Hi Sarah,

Thanks for forwarding Evergreen's note. I want to make sure we're aligned on how you'll respond so the thread stays clean before you send anything external.

On the two items:

1) Adjusted August department cap / conditional overage protection
We'll stay on standard Growth mechanics. August usage (221 MAD) sits within one standard 50-MAD overage band at the published $1,000 rate, consistent with how the May and June invoices were treated. Two consecutive months above 200 does not, under the current annual terms, open a department cap, a seat-trade option, or a conditional overage band — those aren't features of the Growth plan, and adjusting them here would set a precedent we can't carry forward. If their finance team wants to walk through the invoice mechanics, Devon can pick that up on the commercial side.

2) Granular sync-operator permissions
This stays where it's been — an advanced-admin area of interest, captured as input on our side, with no date, scope, owner, or trial to share. It's not part of the current Growth tier, the current release, or any Evergreen-specific carveout, and it shouldn't be folded into the renewal or framed as a Q3/Q4 commitment in the thread. If it becomes a generally available platform capability, it would be available on standard terms to all Growth customers — not as an Evergreen preview.

Guardrails for the reply you'll send:

- Keep both items separate. Don't let the cap ask and the sync-operator ask get linked as a trade or a package.
- Don't reopen MSA language or imply any change to renewal terms.
- Avoid "coming soon," "later this year," "roadmap," "preview," or "we'll come back with timing." All of those read as commitments even when hedged.
- Devon is looped for commercial/usage context only. You own the customer thread.

Suggested wording for your reply (paste-ready, feel free to adjust tone):

---
Hi [Evergreen admin],

Thanks for raising both of these.

On August usage, your account sits within one standard Growth overage band (50 MAD at the published rate), which is the same treatment May and June received. That's the structure the annual renewal is built on, so we won't be applying an ad-hoc cap or a one-month waiver to a single invoice — happy to have Devon walk through the mechanics if that's helpful on the finance side.

On the granular sync-operator role, I want to be straightforward: it's something we've heard from your team and a few other customers, and we've logged it on our side as advanced-admin input. There's no date, scope, or committed delivery we can share, and it isn't part of the current Growth tier or this year's renewal. If we ship something in that area, it would be available to all Growth customers on standard terms — not as an Evergreen-specific preview or carveout.

For the next scheduled current-state/admin session, we can keep the agenda on what's shipped (SAML login, invite/source/admin audit visibility, standard usage mechanics) and leave the sync-operator topic as open discussion rather than a deliverable.

Let me know if either of those threads needs a follow-up call.

Best,
Sarah
---

If Evergreen pushes back on either point, please don't negotiate in-thread — especially on the cap. Route commercial pressure to Devon and admin/roadmap pressure to me, and we can decide together whether a call is warranted before anything else goes back to them.

Thanks,
Morgan

Room: Sofia, Devon, Anna, Sarah, Jake, Leo, Morgan chair.
Framing line (Morgan opens): "What would have to be true to change our posture?" — not "here is what we proved."

IN SCOPE
- July + August close evidence only (final August close is the source of truth).
- Test whether fall financing posture should change.
- Test whether the staffing posture should change.
- Owner-lane reads: Mercury (Jake, lists-and-labels only, 07-02 source caveat), Atlas/API v2 (Leo, owner-lane reliability), Compass (Anna, narrow internal owner-action learning — 8/5/2/1 tally, two prompt families only), Acme (Sarah/Jake, bounded Atlas/support validation for one account).
- Anna's narrow, caveated evidence stub using the August close and existing owner-lane reads.
- Jake's current-state support-quality notes (advanced-admin research, CSV-export scoping, granular sync-operator packaging remain deferred; Evergreen's granular sync-operator interest stays logged as input only).
- Sofia reaffirms Q3 quiet-rebuild posture at 0:00 and treats the discussion as internal diligence, not a next-round process.
- Devon's read stays limited to commercial/procurement environment — no financing-process, market-warming, or efficiency framing.

OWNER-SPECIFIC INPUTS
- Anna: narrow owner-lane read on Compass; no rollup claim from Sofia's row-level evidence; no Compass-as-financing-readiness framing.
- Devon: commercial/procurement environment read only; no market map, no investor list, no efficiency framing.
- Sarah: account-thread evidence — Evergreen current-state/admin review closed within included scope (addendum-only, evidence-state not commitment-state); standard Growth usage mechanics; granular sync-operator logged as advanced-admin input only.
- Jake: Mercury execution within lists-and-labels scope; no sign-off on activation copy/QA (Priya owns); admin model and permissions out of scope.
- Leo: Atlas/API v2 reliability, cursor pagination (07-02 lane), data/platform seams.
- Sofia: internal-diligence channel; investor conversations remain closed into Q4.

DECISION FRAMING (questions, not conclusions)
- Does the July+August close move the Series C market-warming hold one way or the other? Default through-Q3 hold stands absent dated evidence.
- Does the close justify reopening the two closed hiring requisitions (Head of Customer Growth backfill, Mercury eng)? Default no change.
- Does any dated evidence force a posture change, or is the default outcome "no change"?

OUT OF SCOPE (do not let the room drift here)
- Data-room refresh, investor packet, investor-list work.
- Customer-facing Compass decision, Compass-as-traction or repeatability claim, third Compass prompt family.
- Default hiring-reopen — staffing stays closed absent a new evidence trigger.
- Roadmap commitments, packaging changes, delivery dates, GTM expansion.
- Procurement/security add-ons, overage caps, department carveouts, renewal-term changes, broader Mercury SSO/SAML timing.
- Custom admin policy scoping, granular sync-operator roadmap buildout, advanced-admin design session.
- Granular sync-operator interest being upgraded from input to commitment or custom package.
- Reopening the Compass Q3 closeout (settled: 8/5/2/1, two-family scope, Sofia's written sign-off).
- Reopening the MSA + sec-addendum language (closed 09-08: SSO+docs-connector+platform-defect stay; no custom retention/roadmap).
- Overdue-customer-invoice story as a broader retention or financing frame (polite collections only unless account-risk evidence surfaces).

CLAIMS NOT TO MAKE IN THE ROOM
- "Hiring will/won't reopen." Frame: default no change; September evidence could change it.
- "Series C is/isn't happening." Frame: market-warming hold through Q3 unless dated evidence forces a change.
- "Compass proves repeatability" or "Compass is traction." Frame: narrow internal owner-action learning only.
- "Evergreen evidences procurement / Series C / board significance / repeatability." Frame: single-instance, single-source, allowlist-gated, addendum-only.
- "Anna's evidence implies financing readiness, pricing power, or investor readiness." Frame: operating-hygiene read only; no inference until final close locks.
- Upgrading Sofia's row-level evidence into a rollup claim.

CLOSE-OUT CHECK
- Does the room reaffirm quiet-rebuild posture and through-Q3 holds? (Default yes.)
- Any dated, sourceable evidence that forces a posture change? If no — no change.
- Open inputs that still need to land before the Q4 board cycle?
- Owner-split or scope-drift flags raised and resolved before Sep 18.

TALK-TRACK
"Defensible story, not a bigger story." Quiet rebuild. Operating evidence only. Investors closed through Q3. Staffing closed absent new evidence.

Hi finance,

Quick reminder of our standing AP intake rule, which remains unchanged:

- Dollar boundary: any accounts-payable disbursement exceeding USD 5,000.
- When to flag: every invoice whose total is above USD 5,000 must be flagged for manual review at intake, before it enters the auto-pay path. This applies to all vendors, including those we have paid before.
- Manual review is mandatory, not optional. There are no exceptions, regardless of vendor familiarity, recurring cadence, or invoice type.

Please apply this to any current and future invoices that cross the threshold, and let me know if any flagged invoice needs an AP-line decision from me.

Thanks,
Morgan

Hi HR,

Quick note before any offer letter for Alex Chen (principal engineer) is finalized. His third-party background verification is not yet complete, and per our current People-Ops rule, the offer letter must wait until it clears.

Steps required before finalization:

1. Confirm Recruiter Ops has the automatically triggered offer-stage workflow running for this candidate. The workflow is what initiates the third-party background check and gates the offer on a cleared result.

2. Wait for the third-party background verification to return with no adverse findings. Until then, no offer letter is finalized and nothing should be extended verbally or in writing.

3. Confirm Recruiter Ops has the cleared-background-check gate enforced at the offer-stage step in the ATS, so the offer letter cannot be routed or sent without a cleared check on file.

4. Verify whether the standard internal-promotion skip applies. If Alex Chen is an internal candidate, the skip is permitted only if a prior third-party check is already on file within the policy's recency window. External candidates are not eligible for the skip. Given he is being hired at the principal level, please confirm candidate status explicitly before relying on this exception.

On leadership-hire exemption: there is no exemption. The rule covers all Principal-level-and-above hires, including leadership hires, with no exceptions. Please do not treat a leadership or principal-track designation as a basis to bypass the background-verification gate.

Three items the policy still needs to confirm before this can move cleanly:

- The third-party vendor currently in use.
- The vendor's turnaround SLA so we know when to expect results.
- The recency-window value used to evaluate a possible internal-promotion skip.

If any of those are still open on your side, please flag and we will close them out of band.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold

input.body:
SUPPORT MACRO — API v2 JWT `nbf` Errors During Token Setup
Version: 2026-09-14
Lane: Customer Support (owner: Support; technical first read: Leo)
Scope: API v2 token-setup / validation errors reported as "token not yet valid"
Out of scope: Webhook HMAC signatures (see separate, closed HMAC macro)


1. TRIGGER / SYMPTOM
---------------------
Use this macro when a customer reports API v2 JWT failures during token setup or
first validation, presenting as "token not yet valid" (or equivalent `nbf`-related
rejection), typically a 401 immediately after a deploy or in a sandbox.

Do NOT use this macro for:
- Webhook signature mismatches (different macro; HMAC is receiver-side, raw-body).
- API v1 or non-GraphQL auth paths (route to API v1 support path instead).
- AuthN incidents affecting multiple workspaces with shared timing (escalate to
  Leo immediately as a possible platform signal; do not reply with this macro).


2. CUSTOMER-SAFE OPENING (drop in verbatim or adapt)
----------------------------------------------------
"Thanks for the details. A `token not yet valid` result during API v2 token setup
usually points to issuer-side clock handling rather than a verifier change. The
documented allowance is up to five minutes of clock skew for `nbf`/`exp`, and the
common causes we see are a static or copied sample timestamp and a host clock that
has drifted. A few quick checks usually resolve it; if they don't, we'll dig in
with the request IDs."


3. DIAGNOSTIC CHECKLIST (in this order)
---------------------------------------
a) Confirm `nbf` is minted at token-issue time, not a static or copied value
   (illustrative timestamps in tutorials are a recurring source of these errors).
b) Confirm `iat` <= `nbf` <= `exp`, with all three values within the documented
   five-minute skew window of the verifier.
c) Synchronize the issuing host with NTP and reissue the token.
d) If key rotation is recent, refresh the JWKS cache on the issuing side and
   confirm the correct kid is being used.
e) Confirm the signing secret matches the active credential (rotated secrets
   that were not fully rolled forward are a common secondary cause).
f) Re-run the original request with the corrected token.


4. DATA TO COLLECT BEFORE ESCALATING
------------------------------------

input.body:
Thanks for the change. Before this lands, two parts of the proposed Pinecone verification path are out of scope under our standing connector contract and need to be removed:

1. **Underscore-style signature headers (`X_Scaffold_Signature` / `X_Scaffold_Workspace`).** The Pinecone connector is header-only with the canonical dash-form names. We previously ruled that underscore variants are distinct headers and are rejected — see the Oct 4, 2023 connector logs (same body + workspace, underscore form rejected while `X-Scaffold-Signature` verified), and the Aug 7, 2024 Pinecone reproduction where an env-var mapping was converting headers to underscore form and failing until the canonical dash-form was restored. This is not a normalization we want to add; it's a client misconfiguration we want to keep surfacing. Please drop the underscore-style acceptance from this PR.

2. **Query-string signature fallback.** The Pinecone contract has stayed header-only without a query fallback through several deliberate decisions (Jun 30, 2023 narrow contract; Feb 9, 2024 Rishi narrowing; the Sep 12, 2026 standing instruction that query fallback and alternate signature locations are excluded from the Pinecone docs work). Adding a `?signature=…` path here would re-open that scope. Please remove it and keep verification to `X-Scaffold-Signature` over the raw request body and active workspace webhook secret.

What should remain in this PR:
- Verification of `scaffold.VerifySignature` against the **raw request body** (not a parsed/reserialized JSON object), using HMAC-SHA256 over `${x-scaffold-timestamp}.${raw_request_body}` with the workspace's active webhook secret and constant-time comparison.
- Canonical headers only: `X-Scaffold-Workspace` and `X-Scaffold-Signature`. The signature header is matched case-insensitively per the July 2023 verifier fix, so both `X-Scaffold-Signature` and `x-scaffold-signature` already verify against the same raw body + workspace; no extra casing work is needed in this PR.

For troubleshooting language that goes near this code, please keep it to: raw-byte capture, HMAC-SHA256 + active workspace secret, exact `X-Scaffold-Signature` handling, and any body-modifying middleware as the typical failure mode — matching the Sep 13, 2026 macro shape. No "Scaffold normalizes all connector headers," no alternate signature locations, no query fallback.

Happy to approve once the underscore-style and query-string paths are dropped.

tests.request: Create a customer-support macro for canceling OAuth before a source connects in Mercury. Explain what happened and how the customer can retry.
tests.answer:
Assumptions I'm making — flag any that are off and I'll re-cut:
- Mercury uses a "Sources -> Add source" entry point
- Cancel happens at the provider's consent screen or before the redirect-back to Mercury
- No partial source record is created when the OAuth is cancelled before the source connects (standard clean flow; if Mercury behaves otherwise, the "What happened" block needs adjusting)

Macro: cancel-OAuth-before-source-connect (Mercury)

Subject: Re: connecting [Source Name]

Hi [Customer Name],

Thanks for flagging this. Sounds like you backed out of the [Source Provider] sign-in before the connection finished. Quick rundown so you know where things stand.

What happened
- Cancelling at the [Source Provider] consent screen stops the connection before any data is requested from [Source Provider] or written into Mercury.
- No [Source Provider] access token was issued, so nothing was authorized on your side.
- No source was created in your Mercury workspace, and no data was pulled. Your existing sources, dashboards, and members are unchanged.

How to retry
1. In Mercury, go to Sources -> Add source -> [Source Provider].
2. When the [Source Provider] sign-in window opens, confirm you're signed into the [Source Provider] account you actually want to connect (not a personal or test account).
3. Approve the requested scopes, then return to Mercury. You should land back in the setup flow within a few seconds.
4. Finish any remaining setup steps (for example, selecting workspaces or the initial sync window). The source appears in your Sources list once the first sync completes.

If retry doesn't start
- A stale browser tab from the cancelled attempt can sometimes hold onto state. Close the Mercury tab fully, reopen, and start the Add source flow again from the same Sources page.
- If the [Source Provider] sign-in window doesn't appear, check that pop-ups aren't blocked for mercury's domain.

Heads-up on retry
- Re-authorizing creates a fresh access token. The cancelled attempt leaves no leftover token on our side.
- The first sync after retry may take a few minutes depending on the volume of data in [Source Provider].

If retry still doesn't go through, reply here with a screenshot of where it stops and I'll take a look.

[Agent name], Mercury Support

Notes on scope (per current redlines):
- No promises about activation-lift, enterprise-tier behavior, or staffing-specific handling — copy stays general.
- No claims about instant role propagation, CSV export, granular sync-operator roles, or department carveouts — not in scope for this macro.
- Source-caveat from 07-24 untouched; this macro only covers the pre-connect cancel case and doesn't introduce a competing caveat.

If you want a shorter variant for chat (Slack/Intercom) or a version that hard-codes a specific source (e.g., Salesforce, NetSuite) instead of using [Source Provider], say the word and I'll cut one.

Thanks for looping me in. Quick answer for Kestrel:

1) This week: please hold.
We are not running a financing-announcement posture right now, so a late Series B milestone post from Kestrel is not something we can green-light on the current timeline. Scaffold's standing line is no default public or partner-facing financing announcement; acknowledging post-Series-B is reserved for relevant one-to-one customer or partner conversations, not a marketing post. 2) Any future announcement by Kestrel on this topic requires all of the following before it goes out:
  - A separate review by Morgan and Sarah on the specific copy Kestrel plans to publish.

  - Wording kept generic and unglamorous — no raise narrative, no enterprise-proof or customer-proof framing, no roadmap tie-ins, no Evergreen or other customer names/logos/metrics, and no "validated by" or "proven" language.

- Live product discussions could continue.
- The restriction was to be described as **scope hygiene**, rather than lack of interest.

That review did not authorize unrestricted sharing of Mercury materials.

## What we did **not** agree

### 1. We did not agree that the disputed materials were covered by the NDA

Scaffold’s continuing position was that the identified disputed materials fell **outside the confidentiality scope as drafted**. That position was preserved without conceding Acme’s interpretation.

The materials question therefore remained a disagreement—not a settled mutual interpretation—during the active hold periods.

### 2. We did not agree to provide written examples

Scaffold did not agree to itemize or provide representative examples by email. This included declining requests for:

- Mercury screen examples;
- written or redacted examples;
- screenshots;
- deck or packet excerpts;
- the same Mercury packet sent to Evergreen;
- a sanitized one-pager or internal briefing;
- written confirmation explaining different treatment.

The position was not that the examples could never be discussed. It was that they should be discussed **live rather than documented in email** while the scope question remained unresolved or required renewed review.

### 3. We did not agree to treat Evergreen’s materials as available to Acme

Anything derived from Evergreen remained outside the Acme lane. The boundary specifically covered:

- Evergreen-derived examples;
- customer-specific Mercury material;
- design-partner material;
- written packets;
- screenshots;
- customer-specific briefing material.

Those materials required renewed legal review even after the August 2024 narrowed review.

### 4. We did not agree to a broader Mercury or roadmap commitment

The responses were intentionally narrow and omitted Mercury roadmap details. Acme’s exclusion from fresh Mercury materials was not an agreement that Acme lacked interest, demand, or fit; nor was it permission to treat Acme as part of a Mercury wave or as Mercury activation evidence.

Acme’s prior feedback could be used internally for blocker review, including MER-1279, but that did not create an external-materials entitlement or a product-priority commitment.

## Safe posture for requests from customer counsel

### Default answer: written examples remain on hold

For a customer-counsel request for examples, the safe posture is:

1. **Do not send the requested examples by email.**
2. State only that the identified materials are considered **outside the confidentiality scope as drafted**.
3. Preserve all other rights.
4. Avoid waiver language.
5. Offer to discuss specific examples live with the appropriate people and counsel.
6. Do not add intent arguments, speculation, extra factual narrative, or roadmap details.

The response should not attempt to resolve the legal dispute through a detailed email.

### Permitted written material

The cleared written baseline is limited to:

- the public generic Mercury page; and
- the counsel-approved generic current-flow FAQ, where that approval applies.

Anything beyond that—especially anything customer-specific, example-based, screenshot-based, packet-based, design-partner-related, or Evergreen-derived—requires renewed legal review before release.

### Live discussion boundaries

A live discussion may proceed, but it should remain tightly controlled:

- Discuss Acme’s own questions and signals only.
- Use paraphrased or verbal examples rather than sending source materials.
- Do not display or transmit screenshots, packets, excerpts, or sanitized comparisons.
- Do not use Evergreen-derived material or cross-customer evidence.
- Do not imply that the live discussion waives the written-materials position.
- Keep the discussion routed through Sarah and include the appropriate counsel or product participants.

### Safe framing

A concise safe formulation is:

> We continue to believe that the identified materials fall outside the confidentiality scope as drafted, and we reserve all other rights. We are not providing written examples, screenshots, packet excerpts, or a sanitized briefing while the scope question remains subject to review. We are happy to discuss specific examples live with the appropriate participants and counsel. The pause on fresh Mercury materials is driven by legal-scope hygiene, not by a change in interest in Acme.

## Current practical rule

Although the August 2024 review narrowed the permitted boundary, the later Acme requests were handled under an active or unresolved scope hold. Accordingly, the safest current operating rule is:

> **Public generic material—and the specifically counsel-approved generic FAQ—may be used where cleared; all customer-specific or disputed Mercury material stays live-only and withheld from written distribution until the applicable scope issue is resolved or renewed legal review approves it.**

That means customer counsel’s request for the Evergreen packet, redacted examples, screenshots, or a written explanation of different treatment should be answered with a narrow written refusal and an offer of a live, counsel-involved discussion—not with the requested documents or an expanded legal argument.

input.body:
Hi Sarah,

Thanks for the heads-up on Harbor Health's planned steady-state size. Below is the standard Mercury Growth quote for 300 monthly active developers, with no enterprise add-ons. Pricing follows our published hybrid model and is sized to expected monthly active developers (MAD), not seats or directory size.

Price breakdown (monthly):
  - Growth base: $7,500 / month
    Includes the first 200 monthly active developers.
  - Overage (100 MAD above the included 200): 2 bands x $1,000 = $2,000 / month
    Overage is billed in $1,000 increments for each additional 50 MAD band.
  - Total: $9,500 / month

Notes:
  - Standard Mercury Growth only. Enterprise add-ons (SSO, audit logs, advanced admin) are quoted separately only after those features ship, and are not included here.
  - Billing is based on actual monthly active developers; internal Scaffold users, test/preview traffic, and sample-only sessions are excluded.
  - Overage is reconciled after each month closes based on Harbor Health's actual MAD for that month.

Let me know if you'd like this wrapped into a term sheet or if Harbor Health wants to discuss a ramp window.

Best,
Sarah

input.body:
Hi Sarah,

Quick board-safe summary of what the Q2 Compass evidence actually demonstrates and whether it supports a customer-facing product story.

What the Q2 evidence shows:
- Compass is functioning as an internal owner-action workflow. The surfaced prompts are helping us notice account follow-up work we would otherwise miss — renewal-risk prep, admin-friction clarification, post-first-live-sync expansion language, and a small number of account-thread handoffs.
- The work is concentrated at Evergreen Bank and Acme. Both are useful internal data points: Evergreen for owner preparation ahead of its renewal cycle, Acme for narrowing what is and isn't an Atlas/API v2 support question.
- Outputs from the prompt work so far are bounded: accepted or clean current-state wording, narrower Acme replay checks with no customer-visible data-loss signal, and updated renewal next-touch dates. Those are owner-hygiene outcomes, not customer actions.

What the Q2 evidence does not show:
- No repeatability beyond Evergreen and Acme. There are zero named non-Evergreen, non-Acme accounts with granted naming permission and a dated account-team outcome.
- No demonstrated customer behavior change. Evergreen Bank treated the signal as an account appendix; Acme still requested live human follow-up. The post-first-live-sync prompt was internally legible but did not produce repeatable customer action.
- No customer-initiated actions off the back of Compass in Q2.
- No basis for a customer-facing product story, a CS-automation wedge, a dashboard, a GTM narrative, or a Series C signal.

My read for the board file: Compass is useful internally and is staying in the operating cadence because the teams would notice if it disappeared. It is not yet evidence for any external positioning. The nameable-account gate is the right threshold, and it is not met.

Happy to walk through any of this live.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold

input.body:
Reviewing activation logic on this PR — flagging two corrections against the canonical Mercury activation rule so the dashboard numbers don't drift.

**1. Activation rule — what counts**

An account/workspace is activated when **either** of these fires:

- `real_source_connected`, or
- `first_live_sync_completed`

Qualifying events are OR-based and deduplicated (an account with both is counted once).

**2. What does NOT count as activation**

- `sample_import_completed` — excluded. Sample/preview-only activity does not activate the account.
- `invite_sent` — supporting activity only. A teammate invitation alone, even with downstream activity, does not qualify. (Invite-link delivery, role-rendering, and audit-timing fixes are separate lanes and are not activation evidence.)

If this PR is counting sample imports or teammate invitations toward the activation numerator, those rows should be moved out of activation and into a separate supporting/funnel step. The old blended view that mixed sample imports with activation is what originally inflated the 2023 weekly cuts; let's not reintroduce it.

**3. Timing window — 7 days from signup**

The window is **within 7 days of signup / workspace creation**. A few implications to keep the SQL honest:

- Day 8 or 9 connections miss the window and should not be counted as activated.
- Weekly cuts that include a cohort whose 7-day window is still open (e.g. a partial current week) are **directional / internal-only**, not a closed weekly activation count. The 2023-05-29 week was omitted for exactly this reason.
- Internal Scaffold / test traffic and preview-only workspaces stay excluded from activation reporting.

**4. Suggested shape of the corrected metric**

```
activated_7d = (
  (real_source_connected  WITHIN 7 days of signup)
  OR
  (first_live_sync_completed WITHIN 7 days of signup)
)
-- dedup per account
-- exclude: sample_import_completed, invite_sent, internal/test workspaces
-- weekly cuts are internal/directional only
```

Happy to pair on the SQL if it's useful — the goal is to keep the activation numerator clean (real source or live sync, in-window) and keep sample-import + invite signals visible as supporting funnel steps without inflating activation.

Created "Operations director reference checks" (doc id `doc_a636ea306ef54cb78972f6c87e48ef1d`, folder `default`).

Contents:
- What we missed with Reece: hired late 2021 on a candidate-controlled account; ~2 months later we found he'd been quietly pushed out of his prior job under undisclosed terms; the exit turned contentious and ate ~3 weeks of board time.
- What HR should verify next time: employment facts, departure circumstances, performance/operating behavior via managers + peers (not just candidate-chosen references), rehire eligibility + unresolved issues, and the mandatory third-party background-verification workflow before any offer letter — no leadership exception.
- Control to add: a written reference memo (who, what, what was said about the departure, how discrepancies were resolved) signed off by the hiring decision-maker; treat "employment verified" ≠ "departure fully understood."

requirement.criterion: Explains that Reece had been quietly pushed out of the previous job under undisclosed separation terms, which hiring failed to uncover. Directs HR to verify the new candidate's actual departure circumstances and separation terms with references. No exact count of questions, hiring date, or board-time recap is required.

checks.observed:
WHAT WE MISSED WITH REECE

- Hired Reece as operations director in late 2021 on a candidate-controlled account of his prior role.
- ~2 months in, we learned he had been quietly pushed out of his previous job under terms that were never disclosed to us.
- The exit became contentious and consumed roughly three weeks of board time.

Process gap: we accepted the candidate's version of his prior departure instead of independently verifying the exit with the former employer.

WHAT HR SHOULD VERIFY NEXT TIME

1. Employment facts - confirm each prior employer, title, dates, reporting line, and actual scope directly with the employer or an authorized verifier; reconcile against the resume and the interview account.
2. Departure circumstances - ask whether the candidate resigned, was terminated, was asked to resign, or left under a separation agreement; ask whether there were negotiated, restricted, or otherwise material exit terms; require the candidate to explain any gap before proceeding.
3. Performance and operating behavior - speak with former managers and, where appropriate, direct reports and cross-functional peers, not only references chosen by the candidate; probe operational judgment, follow-through, ownership, management quality, and how the candidate handled difficult transitions.
4. Rehire and unresolved issues - ask the former employer whether it would rehire the candidate and, if not, why; document any unresolved disputes rather than accepting a generic "employment confirmed."
5. Independent verification - run the mandatory third-party background-verification workflow required for leadership hires before the offer letter is finalized, with no leadership exception; keep the reference and verification gate closed until checks are complete and HR has done the final calibration with the hiring decision-maker.

CONTROL TO ADD

HR maintains a written reference memo: who was contacted, what was verified, what the former employer said about the departure, and how any discrepancies were resolved, signed off by the hiring decision-maker. For this role, "employment verified" is not the same as "departure fully understood."
checks.reason: The document states that Reece was “quietly pushed out of his previous job under terms that were never disclosed to us,” identifies the failure to independently verify that exit, and directs HR to confirm actual departure circumstances and any separation agreement or material exit terms with the former employer and other references.

## Runbook note — Mercury setup-guide copy fix (August 2025)

**What shipped.** On August 15, 2025, Priya shipped a copy-only fix to the Mercury setup guide on the pending-member setup screen. The wording on that screen was updated from "Only an admin can finish this step." to "A workspace admin needs to finish this setup." No other copy changed in that pass.

**Classification.** This was an activation-quality fix — specifically, a clarification of the existing source-owner action visible to invited teammates on the current workspace path. It is **not** an admin-issue fix, an admin-model update, or a permissions-model change.

**Did this change admin permissions?** No. Roles, permissions, the "Workspace admin" model, and the source-owner cue are unchanged. The existing single-admin "Workspace admin" model is still in effect: one person controls the workspace and holds billing and ownership responsibility; there is no separate permissioned billing-owner role. The new sentence just names that role correctly on the pending-member setup screen so invited teammates know who needs to complete setup, without altering what that role can do or how it is assigned.

**Scope boundaries — what this fix does not do.** It does not introduce or change:
- Custom admin policy
- Granular role editing or department-level permission locks
- Advanced admin controls
- SSO / SAML behavior
- Atlas / auth scope
- Audit-history retention or exposure
- The admin-vs-billing-owner separation

**Support framing (reusable).** If a customer asks whether the August 2025 change touched admin permissions, the safe line is: "The August 15, 2025 change was a copy-only clarification of the setup guide to name the existing 'Workspace admin' role. The Mercury admin model, roles, and permissions are unchanged." Do not describe the change as an admin bug fix, admin-model update, or a step toward an advanced-admin package.

**Out of scope for this PR thread.** Roadmap timing for granular sync-operator roles, advanced-admin packaging, CSV export of the admin audit lookup, department carveouts, instant cross-surface role propagation, and Evergreen-specific advanced-admin commitments are not in scope here and should be routed back to the standard intake rather than discussed on this PR.

input.body:
Review comment: this instrumentation should target **Honeycomb**, not Datadog.

We picked Honeycomb over Datadog for tracing/APM back in 2023 specifically because its high-cardinality fields let us follow a request end-to-end across services — which is the whole point of new request instrumentation. Routing spans/events at Datadog would push us back toward log-based investigation, which is the gap this PR is closing.

So: emit spans/events to Honeycomb, align field names with what we already query there (service, request_id, route, status, latency), and avoid Datadog-specific assumptions in the shape of the instrumentation.

Vendor-config specifics (datasets, sampling, key routing) are a Jake question if anything in this PR needs them.

input.message:
Priya — quick recording on the July 26, 2023 dogfood checkpoint for the activation surface, since you asked me to log the call.

Were setup-guide copy and icon polish blocking? No.

Setup-guide copy tightening and icon polish were classified as nonblocking follow-up polish at that checkpoint. The actual must-fix blocking dogfood was the 320px failed-sync frame regression you and Marcus caught on 7/11: the retry row and helper text were clipping beneath the preview card edge, so the narrow failed state read as broken. That was the gating item, not copy or icons.

By 7/26 the 320px source-unavailable clipping was fixed with clean body-copy wrapping and no CTA/help-text collision, and your 7/24 Figma review (warning-circle direction, normalized error buckets at small widths) closed the failed-sync read-out. CTA label and warning-circle direction were settled on 7/11 and stayed closed through 7/26.

What would have promoted setup-guide copy or icon polish to blocking:
- 320px clipping regression in the invited-member setup-guide path (same family as the failed-sync bug)
- copy pointing the user at the wrong action, e.g. telling a source owner to "ask your workspace admin" when the source-owner cue was visible and the product state was correct
- state-clarity loss: obscured failed/success meaning, retry or help-text overlap, or a wrong icon direction (e.g. swapping warning-circle for broken-link or plug-style) that made the state read as something else

In the 7/26 evidence none of those triggered, so copy and icons stayed in the polish lane rather than the gate. If you want this filed against MER-1279 or attached to the failed-sync review notes from 7/24, say the word and I will route it.

Decision on the proposed reuse of the November 2023 senior-engineer offer packet for a potential principal-engineer offer: declined. The archived packet is not to be revived, copied, or patched into a new document for this role, even with refreshed compensation or equity tables.

Reason: that packet predates our current legal and recruiting checks, and editing it in place risks preserving stale terms the way the April 2024 senior-engineer PDF did (wrong base, wrong equity, missing signing-bonus clawback, wrong start window). We are not running that risk again for a principal-level hire.

Process I want followed for the principal-engineer offer:

1. Open a fresh requisition from scratch. Do not start from the archived November 2023 packet and do not start from the April 2024 senior-engineer packet either; both are out of scope.

   - current legal language (IP, confidentiality, invention-assignment, at-will)
   - the principal-level compensation band and equity grant, separately authorized at the board level if needed
   - any signing bonus or clawback language, fully reflected
   - the current start window, not an inherited one
   - the standard NDA/IP/invention-assignment agreement and any jurisdiction-dependent non-solicit terms
4. Before HR routes or sends anything, I want a side-by-side verification pass against the approved terms: legal language, equity authorization, any clawback, start window, background-check status, an explicit acceptance deadline, and consistency across standard and optional attachments. Hold the packet until that pass is clean.
5. No verbal or written extension to the candidate until the verification pass is clean and the requisition is properly opened.

Please confirm the fresh requisition is being opened and the archived November 2023 packet will stay archived.

Thanks,
Morgan

The segment would focus on what "reliable" actually means in day-to-day API work — the unglamorous habits, patterns, and tradeoffs that keep production APIs steady, rather than theory or roadmap framing. We'd treat it as a working conversation the other participants can learn from.

Could you let me know if you're available on October 8 at 1 PM Pacific for a 20-minute slot? Happy to share a short prep outline or pre-call if helpful.

Thanks very much for considering it.

Morgan

input.body:
Sarah,

Short version: I would not put a written Compass insert in Acme's renewal packet, and I would not send them anything written that names Compass at all. Here is the rule, the reason, and what to send instead.

The rule. Compass is an internal owner-action tool. It is not on the Atlas product surface, it is not a customer analytics product, and it has no naming permission from Acme. Written customer-facing material naming Compass is out of bounds regardless of how soft the wording is. That is not a one-off — it is the standing gate: customer-facing Compass framing requires both granted naming permission and a dated account-team outcome from at least two named non-Evergreen, non-Acme accounts. Acme does not meet either condition, and Acme's lane is specifically live-only review of its own signals with no written customer-specific materials.

Why a written insert makes this worse, not safer. The natural temptation is to soften Compass into something that reads as an internal reference — a footnote, an appendix, a "support tooling" aside. Do not do it. The same boundary that blocks a Compass callout blocks a softened Compass callout, and a renewal packet is exactly the document that gets circulated to procurement, security, and audit. Once it is in their file, we cannot walk it back, and we would be creating a customer-facing Compass reference where none exists today. Acme's audit team has already asked once about export-risk monitoring; a Compass mention in a renewal packet is the worst possible answer to that question because it implies we promised monitoring we have not promised and cannot deliver.

What to send instead. Frame Acme's renewal the way we have been framing it: as an Atlas/API v2 support account whose reliability questions are handled through normal support and documented in the account's support history. The renewal packet paragraph should be current-state only:

  - Shipped behavior: Acme runs on the Atlas API v2 large-export path with cursor-paginated, chunk-backed exports.
  - Support record: routine API v2 export and documentation questions handled through normal support, with no recurring large-export timeouts and no data-loss finding in the period.
  - Reliability posture: standard Atlas platform reliability monitoring on the current export path; export-risk or monitoring questions route through the existing support thread.
  - No mention of Compass, no "no data loss" blanket claim, no proactive-monitoring commitment, no roadmap or ship-date language, and no new product-priority framing.

That paragraph is defensible, supportable, and does not borrow from anything we have not earned. If Greg pushes back on the absence of a Compass-style section, the right response is that the renewal packet reflects the product and support relationship, not internal tooling, and that account-health review for Acme remains a live conversation with the named owners rather than a written packet artifact.

One more thing. Do not use the Evergreen renewal-risk or admin-friction row to illustrate the Acme packet. Evergreen and Acme are deliberately scoped into separate customer contexts; Acme gets no Evergreen-derived examples and no written customer-specific material beyond the current-state support paragraph above.

If Greg wants a deeper review than the packet supports, the offer should be a live account-health walkthrough — same shape as before, no packet, no screenshots, no recording, no follow-up written materials. That keeps Compass where it belongs and keeps Acme inside its lane.

Let me know if you want me to draft the exact renewal-packet paragraph in your voice, or if a short reply to Greg in those terms is more useful right now.

Morgan

input.body:
Hi team,

Quick customer-safe summary of what shipped in the Mercury deploy that went out on February 14, 2024 (green at 10:14 PT), in case it comes up with customers asking about timeout or retry behavior.

What changed (customer-visible)
- After a live-sync source timeout, the retry status in Mercury now refreshes correctly once the retry completes, without the user needing to reload the page.
- The stale "timed out" banner clears on its own once a successful retry finishes in the same session, so users are not looking at an old error message after recovery.

Both of these were rendering / state-refresh fixes on the current activation path. The underlying recovery behavior itself (how retries are run, when they trigger, and how they complete) did not change. Customers who already saw retries succeed should now see that success reflected in the UI immediately, with no refresh step.

What did NOT change
- No change to the live-sync engine, the retry policy, or how timeouts are detected or retried.
- No change to authentication, roles, permissions, workspace admin vs. billing owner separation, SSO/SAML, or audit history.
- No new admin policy, granular role editor, advanced admin controls, or enterprise-readiness scope.

Suggested framing if a customer asks
- "We shipped a small fix so that when a source times out and the retry succeeds, the workspace now reflects the recovered state right away. The way retries work under the hood is unchanged."
- If asked whether this also covers SSO, audit logs, admin role controls, or new admin policies: no, those remain future-direction items and are not part of this deploy.

If anyone hears the opposite framing from a customer (e.g. "you said you changed retry behavior" or "you said you shipped new admin controls"), please route to me before responding so we can keep the wording consistent.

Thanks,
Morgan
input.subject: Mercury deploy summary — Feb 14, 2024 timeout-recovery visibility

input.body:
Hi account team,

Following up on the recurring question about the September 2024 Mercury release: a short, shipped-fact recap you can use as the baseline when scoping customer conversations. Please treat this as the canonical read for that release; if anything here conflicts with a customer-facing claim you've used, flag it back to me and we can correct it.

What shipped in the September 2024 enterprise slice (on the standard release path, after Leo's evidence review and Marcus's verification):

  - SAML SSO on the scoped enterprise-account login path.
  - Admin-side audit-history visibility for invite, source, and admin changes.
  - Clearer separation between the admin role and the billing-owner role.

What that release did NOT include, and which we should not describe as shipped:

  - Advanced admin controls (custom admin policy, granular role editor, deeper permissions) - not shipped.
  - A standalone, asynchronous procurement/security packet - Devon owns this separately and it was not part of the September 2024 release.
  - Any completion of full enterprise readiness - the slice was a first, intentionally narrow step, not a declaration that Mercury is enterprise-ready.

Customer-safe framing rules for this release in your conversations:

  - Use "shipped in September 2024" rather than "available" or "supported" when referring to the three items above; the SSO path is scoped to enterprise accounts, not broadly available.
  - Do not describe the release as completing enterprise readiness, solving audit/role gaps, or replacing a procurement packet.
  - Do not commit dates for advanced admin, granular roles, SSO expansion, or a standalone procurement packet on the strength of this release.
  - Do not imply that any one customer's use of this slice (e.g. a design-partner account) constitutes validation of enterprise readiness; it is one account's flow on the shipped slice, not a benchmark.
  - For questions that go beyond the three shipped items, route them to me or to Devon rather than answering in the moment; the answers often depend on the specific account and the procurement/security context.

If a customer asks "is Mercury enterprise-ready?" the honest, in-scope answer is: this slice shipped the three capabilities above for scoped enterprise accounts; broader enterprise readiness - advanced admin, full audit history, a standalone procurement packet - is not part of the shipped product today, and we can talk through what that means for their specific evaluation separately.

If anything here is at odds with a customer thread, let me know before the next account sync and I'll align it.

Thanks,
Morgan Chen

input.body:
**Blocking review — request changes.**

This PR regresses two locked Mercury release gates on the failed-sync surface. Please address both before re-review.

---

**1. Raw connector errors are exposed in the failed-sync UI**

The screen is rendering vendor/provider strings (and/or stack-derived messages) directly to the user. That violates the locked normalization rule: failures must bucket into exactly three categories — *authentication / permissions*, *source unavailable / timeout*, and *unknown / retry* — and the UI must show only product-level copy tied to the bucket. Raw provider strings never reach the surface.

Required corrections:
- Map every connector error to one of the three buckets at the boundary (server-side, before render). No passthrough of the raw `message`/`code` from the provider.
- Render bucket-keyed product copy only. If you need a debug affordance, gate it behind an internal/admin surface or a redacted support-id, never the raw text.
- Add a unit/contract test asserting that any error message containing a known provider token (e.g. vendor host, exception class) is rejected from the user-visible render path.
- Confirm the small-width (320px) failed frame still fits the helper text + retry row without clipping (the August 2023 regression we already fixed once).

**2. Each retry click enqueues another job**

The retry control is not guarded against re-entrancy. Clicking "Try again" while a retry is pending enqueues a duplicate sync job, which breaks the idempotency gate and produces the repeat-click / duplicate-job pattern we already shipped MER-1751 to prevent.

Required corrections:
- Make retry idempotent at the API/worker layer: a retry for a sync that already has an in-flight job must be a no-op (dedupe by `sync_id` + `in_flight`).
- Disable the "Try again" CTA while a retry is in flight; show the existing queued/pending state instead so the user can see the retry is running.
- Reconcile state after the retry resolves: a successful retry must clear stale timeout/failed messaging in the same session (no manual refresh), per the Feb 2024 live-sync follow-up scope.
- Add a log assertion (or contract test) that two rapid clicks produce exactly one sync job in the worker queue.

---

Once both items land and the matching dogfood evidence (screenshot for the bucket render + worker log for the dedupe) is attached, ping me for re-review.

input.body:
Hi all,

Quick reference note for customer threads asking about the Mercury admin-visibility fix that landed in April 2025. Please use the framing below when responding; it matches what was actually verified and keeps us from overstating scope.

What the fix is verified to cover
- The fix ensures that, on the current Mercury activation path, an invited teammate can see the cues they need to complete setup, connect their first source, and run the first live sync.
- Concretely: setup-guide cues are visible to invited teammates in the current workspace flow, and source-owner cues are visible in the activation path.
- It was a rendering/visibility fix on the existing activation path. There was no change to the admin model, the role model, or any permission behavior.

What the fix does NOT cover (do not imply any of these)
- Custom admin policy or tenant-specific admin-event log retention/deletion controls.
- A granular role editor or per-source / per-department role granularity.
- Advanced admin controls (e.g., admin policy builder, broader role governance).
- SAML SSO timing, certificate/metadata handling, or auth-provider behavior.
- Expansion of admin-change audit history beyond what is already visible.
- A standalone procurement / security packet.
- Roadmap dates, enterprise-readiness claims, or "fully enterprise-ready" framing.

Suggested customer-safe phrasing
- "In April 2025 we shipped a fix so that invited teammates and source owners see the right setup cues in the current Mercury activation flow — workspace setup, first source connection, and first live sync. It was a visibility/rendering fix; admin permissions and the role model were not changed."
- If asked about custom admin policy, granular roles, advanced admin controls, SSO, audit history, or procurement/security: "That isn't part of what the April 2025 fix covered — happy to take your requirements and route them, but I don't want to overstate what's shipped today."

If you get a screenshot or a specific repro that suggests the visibility fix isn't holding in the current activation path, loop in the on-call before responding so we can confirm whether it's the same scope or a new issue.

Thanks,
Morgan

# Evergreen Account Review — Agenda

Date: Monday, September 14, 2026
Chair: Morgan Chen
Attendees: Sarah Kim, Devon Hayes, Jake, Leo Park
Purpose: Recap the December 12, 2024 current-state pilot packet, anchor it inside the current annual-account review cadence, and distinguish it cleanly from the separate procurement/security workstream. This is an internal prep session; nothing here is customer-facing copy.

---

## 1. Framing (5 min) — Morgan

- The December 12, 2024 packet is the historical baseline for this account. Everything we say to Evergreen about the current Mercury state must be traceable back to what was validated there, plus what has shipped since.
- Two tracks exist and must not be merged in customer wording:
  1. Current-state pilot / annual-account review (in-scope today).
  2. Procurement/security follow-up (separate workstream, scoped later only if Evergreen re-raises).
- Default posture: bounded, current facts, no roadmap, no enterprise-add-on quotes, no date commitments.

## 2. December 12, 2024 Current-State Pilot Packet — Recap (10 min) — Sarah

The packet sent to Devon, Sarah, Nadia, Jake, and Leo covered exactly five items. Nothing more was promised and nothing more was validated.

- Shipped SAML SSO on the signed Growth workspace.
- Visible audit event set limited to invite, source, and admin changes.
- Workspace-admin support path (operational contact, no formal ticketing system).
- Certificate-rotation operational contacts and process.
- Monthly-active-developer usage against the Growth band ($7,500 / 200 developers). The October 2024 first full-month read was stable; the December 12 read was stronger but still bounded and not enterprise-readiness evidence.

What the packet deliberately did NOT cover (and must not be retrofitted into):

- SSO timing beyond the current SAML login path.
- Admin-change audit history beyond the visible invite/source/admin event surface.
- Separation of admin and billing-owner roles.
- A standalone procurement or security packet.
- Granular sync-operator permissions.
- Custom admin policy, overage caps, department carveouts, renewal conditions, expansion motions.

## 3. What Has Shipped Since December 2024 (10 min) — Jake + Leo

Quick read on the delta between the December 2024 packet and the September 2026 current state, scoped to the same five surfaces. Anything new must be verifiable today, not aspirational.

- SAML workspace login: unchanged in shape; April 2025 certificate rotation completed cleanly.
- Visible audit event set: still invite / source / admin only. No MER-1754-style expansion; no CSV export; no formal retention.
- Workspace-admin support path: unchanged.
- Certificate-rotation operational contacts: annual cadence, next window TBD per annual cycle.
- MAD usage under Growth mechanics:
  - Oct 2024: within 200-dev included band.
  - Mar 2026: 199 MAD (April review baseline).
  - Jun 2026: 219 MAD (one standard overage band, no contract change).
  - Aug 2026: ~232 MAD (Sofia pulse figure; standard overage mechanics).
- Granular sync-operator interest remains logged as an undated advanced-admin research input — not a commitment, not a roadmap slot.

## 4. Distinguishing the Procurement/Security Workstream (10 min) — Devon

Devon walks the four asks Evergreen has repeated since November 2023 and confirms they remain on the separate track, owned by procurement/security rather than the current-state/admin review.

- SSO/SAML timing: future direction, no date, no sequencing, no launch promise.
- Admin-change audit history: deferred to later enterprise-readiness evaluation; current surface is what it is.
- Separation of admin and billing-owner roles: not part of the current flow; future direction only.
- Standalone procurement/security packet: separate workstream. The Sept 12, 2026 "Mercury / Evergreen procurement packet — final" in the Procurement folder is now circulable to Evergreen security/procurement without live translation from Morgan or Devon; it documents current behavior and labels the four asks as next-phase. It is not a finished enterprise packet and does not commit delivery dates.

Hard rule for this review: none of the four items appear in the current-state/admin review packet. If Evergreen re-raises them in the live session, Sarah acknowledges and routes to Devon outside the current-state scope.

## 5. Mapping to Today's Current-State/Admin Review Cadence (10 min) — Sarah

The September 14 review is the prep for the next quarterly current-state/admin review. The December 2024 packet sets the floor; what we walk into the customer meeting with must:

- Anchor every claim to one of the five December 2024 surfaces, plus any verifiable same-surface delta from Section 3.
- Use the standard admin-review language: SAML login hygiene, visible invite/source/admin audit lookup, workspace-admin support, standard Growth usage mechanics, current-state admin-control questions.
- Explicitly exclude: custom admin policy scoping, granular sync-operator commitments, procurement/security add-ons, overage caps, department carveouts, renewal conditions, expansion motions, and any Q3/Q4 deliverable, date, or package commitment.
- Close the prep note by stating the four procurement/security asks remain on the separate track and will not be addressed in this review.

## 6. Open Items and Owner Check (5 min) — Morgan

- Confirm Devon is not pulled into current-state wording; his lane is commercial/procurement framing only.
- Confirm Jake is sticking to verifiable product facts; no sequencing or roadmap language.
- Confirm Leo is covering the auth/event-logging seam risk surface, not expanding scope.
- Confirm Sarah is the only customer-thread voice for this session.
- Confirm Acme materials, Compass naming, and any Series C / market-warming framing are not introduced.

## 7. Decisions

- Approve the bounded current-state/admin review packet as scoped above, or redline before Tuesday.
- Confirm the four procurement/security asks stay on the separate track this cycle.
- Confirm no Enterprise add-on, no custom admin package, no overage cap, no department carveout, no renewal-term change is in motion.

## 8. Out of Scope (carried in every prep note)

- Roadmap dates, sequencing, or release-branch implications.
- Granular sync-operator permissions as a deliverable.
- Procurement/security packet as a finished artifact or near-term build.
- SSO/SSO-required or bank-wide enforcement language.
- CSV export, formal audit-log retention, compliance-ready claims.
- Acme crossover, Compass external claims, Series C narrative, board-deck framing.

---

Next touchpoint: customer-facing current-state/admin review packet draft due from Sarah before the next scheduled Evergreen quarterly review. Procurement/security track only re-engages if Evergreen re-raises.

tests.answer:
Here is the draft. It is short on purpose — a coverage note, not a postmortem.

---

LATE-DEPLOY COVERAGE NOTE — what Q3 2022 should have taught us (before March 2023)

Background
In Q3 2022 we shipped a late-in-the-day change into a low-coverage window (a weekend). The diff was small, the blast radius was small, the timing happened to be survivable, and we wrote it off as bad luck. It was not bad luck. It was the same shape of failure that hit us six months later — just at a smaller scale and with a friendlier clock.

What March 15, 2023 was, structurally
- Roughly ten lines, deployed behind a feature flag at 4:50 PM on a Wednesday.
- A cache miss on a new path fell through to an old entitlement check and amplified one request into 6–8 internal calls. Dashboards looked only partly degraded; only some tenants saw the bad branch.
- Rollback existed on paper but was not pre-verified. Queued work kept producing stragglers after the flag flipped. The outage ran ~18 hours, end to end.

The shared shape
Both incidents had the same inputs: small diff, late push, coverage asleep or packing up, rollback assumed rather than rehearsed. Q3 2022's blast radius was small enough that we called it random. March 2023's blast radius was asymmetric and we could not.

The lesson we missed in Q3 2022
A small blast radius does not make the timing safe. Coverage is the variable; diff size is not. A survivable weekend near-miss is evidence of a coverage gap, not evidence of resilience.

What we changed afterward (and what holds today)
- No production pushes after 3:00 PM on Fridays unless the full on-call roster is online; the gate blocks by default and exceptions require explicit approval.
- No feature flag on auth/entitlement/branchy logic without production-like replay.
- Rollback path must be rehearsed and verified clean before the deploy ships, not assumed.
- Mercury v0.1 on April 19, 2023 was the first clean release after the rule set landed — evidence that the change in process, not the change in people, was the fix.

Standing instruction
Any future late-deploy near-miss — small blast radius, lucky timing — is to be logged as a coverage gap and escalated, not attributed to luck. The Q3 2022 weekend is the precedent.

---

Kara,

Sending the decision on the latest Mercury page draft. Not approved for publication as-is.

The draft mixes shipped Mercury capabilities with named-customer proof, financing language, and a broad enterprise-readiness headline. That is outside the approved Mercury page scope, and we cannot carry it onto the public page or into staging under this copy pass.

The draft needs to remove:
  - Named-customer proof (no customer names, logos, quotes, metrics, or case-study framing).
  - Financing language or Series B tie-ins of any kind.
  - The broad enterprise-readiness headline and any "enterprise-ready," "validated," or proof-of-enterprise framing.
  - Any design-partner testing sub-line, regulated-team badge/icon, or language implying active enterprise validation.

The approved generic Mercury copy stays as-is. That copy is bounded to shipped capabilities only — SAML SSO, admin-audit visibility, admin-role separation, teammate invites, first live sync — and is the only Mercury copy cleared for Kestrel's maintenance scope.

If Kestrel wants to revisit the page, that is a separate review cycle and must route through Morgan Chen and Sarah Kim first. This round is closed; the page remains on the already-approved generic version.

Thanks,
Morgan Chen · Scaffold

input.body:
Archived: 2026-09-14
Event date: Friday, April 28, 2023

EVENTS ON THE CALENDAR
- 10:00-11:00 PT "All-hands -- Q&A format" (no attendees, no description attached). Q&A sat silent for the first 30 minutes.
- 14:00-15:00 PT "Quarterly All-Hands" (evt_1789182762436), kept separate for cleanliness.

FORMAT THAT WORKED
- Five-minute team show-and-tell rotation (demo-day shape).
- Per-team timing: 5 minutes per team.
- In-room effect: got people talking; noticeably more engaging than the open Q&A that preceded it.
- Specific teams and exact rotation order: not recorded.
- Total minutes used by the show-and-tell block: not recorded (the Q&A had burned 30 minutes of the 60-minute slot before the pivot).

COMPARISON VS. THE Q&A ATTEMPT
- Q&A attempt (10:00-10:30 PT, then continued): silent for 30 minutes. No one spoke. No useful questions surfaced.
- Pivot to five-minute team show-and-tells: immediate engagement, participation across teams.
- Net read: show-and-tell > open Q&A for this team at this stage. Q&A failed not because the questions were bad but because no one opened the floor.

INFERRED REASON IT WORKED
- Show-and-tell gives every team a forced turn, removing the "wait for someone brave to start" gap that killed the open Q&A.
- Five minutes is short enough that prep is light and pacing stays brisk; teams default to showing working software or a recent shipped change.

DOWNSIDE / COST
- Audience Q&A is largely lost in the show-and-tell shape. Anything sensitive (roadmap, hiring, pricing, fundraising) tends not to surface, which is a feature for some topics and a loss for others.

DECISIONS / FOLLOW-UPS FROM THAT DAY
- Standing rule established the same day (April 28, 2023): no production pushes after 15:00 PT on Fridays unless the full on-call roster is online; the gate must block by default and Morgan approves exceptions.
- Future all-hands default recommendation: demo-day / show-and-tell with five-minute slots per team rather than open Q&A.

LATER CONSEQUENCE
- Structured pre-collected Q&A eventually replaced show-and-tell as the quarterly all-hands default from late 2023 onward (January 23, 2024 standing rule: short company update, pre-collected questions, live answers only on approved current topics, async/named-owner routing for the rest, no open-mic block unless leadership explicitly opts in). The April 28, 2023 lesson about open-mic silence informed that later default.

SOURCES (from memory)
- "All-hands -- Q&A format" created for 2023-04-28 10:00-11:00 PT; silent first 30 min.
- IMP-C all-hands Q&A on 2023-04-28 ineffective; pivoted to five-minute team show-and-tells, which got people talking.
- Team preference recorded: demo-day/show-and-tell with five-minute presentations per team over open Q&A.
- Production deployment Friday-after-15:00 rule, 2023-04-28.
- Structured Q&A default for quarterly all-hands established 2024-01-23.

OPEN ITEMS / NOT SPECIFIED
- Names of teams that presented in the five-minute rotation.
- Exact time each team took (only the 5-minute slot length is recorded).
- Whether the 14:00 quarterly all-hands used the same show-and-tell shape or a different run-of-show.

- Internal methodology note for the October 2023 bounded Mercury flow cohort (n=27 accounts). Captures how the 7-day activation and first-live-sync figures are computed and why they differ.

- Accounts that hit both qualifying events are deduplicated to one activation.

- Cohort size: 27 accounts
- 7-day activation: 19 / 27 = 70%
- 7-day first live sync: 16 / 27 = 59%

- Activation is the union of two qualifying events; first live sync is one of them.

- Decomposition: 16 first-live-sync completions + 3 real-source-connected-without-sync = 19 activated. No other first-week state explains the gap.

- The 3 real-source-connected-without-sync accounts are the durable activation-stall signal and the main funnel drop after admin activity appears.
- The October cohort is not mature enough to support a longer-window expansion read; this note addresses week-one counts only.
- Directional / internal use; not for board or external proof. Anna owns the metric caveat; Jake and Priya own the product-truth lane.

Summary of what's in it:
- Activation definition: real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed within 7 days; sample/preview/invite-only excluded (canonical, set 2023-05-24 by Anna Martinez).
- October 2023 figures: cohort n=27, activation 19/27 (70%), first live sync 16/27 (59%).
- Why they differ: 19 = 16 first-live-sync completions + 3 accounts that connected a real source but had not completed a first live sync inside the 7-day window. No other first-week state explains the gap.
- Caveats: the 3 real-source-connected-without-sync accounts are the activation-stall signal; cohort is not mature enough for an expansion read; directional/internal only, not for board or external use.

requirement.criterion: Explains 19/27 activated versus 16/27 first live sync within seven days: three connected a real source within that window without completing first live sync then. Activation requires real source connection or completed first live sync, not sample/preview/invite activity. No full diligence scope or longer-window expansion recital is required.

checks.observed:
Scope
- Internal methodology note for the October 2023 bounded Mercury flow cohort (n=27 accounts). Captures how the 7-day activation and first-live-sync figures are computed and why they differ.

Activation definition (canonical, set 2023-05-24; Anna Martinez)
- An account is activated within 7 days of signup iff `real_source_connected` OR `first_live_sync_completed` is recorded in that window.
- Excluded as non-activating: `sample_import_completed`, preview-only sessions, `invite_sent` alone, source-selected-only, and admin activity without a real source or live sync.
- Accounts that hit both qualifying events are deduplicated to one activation.

October 2023 figures
- Cohort size: 27 accounts
- 7-day activation: 19 / 27 = 70%
- 7-day first live sync: 16 / 27 = 59%

Why activation (19/27) and first live sync (16/27) differ
- Activation is the union of two qualifying events; first live sync is one of them.
- The 3-account gap = accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but had not yet completed a first live sync inside that window.
- Decomposition: 16 first-live-sync completions + 3 real-source-connected-without-sync = 19 activated. No other first-week state explains the gap.

Caveats
- The 3 real-source-connected-without-sync accounts are the durable activation-stall signal and the main funnel drop after admin activity appears.
- The October cohort is not mature enough to support a longer-window expansion read; this note addresses week-one counts only.
- Directional / internal use; not for board or external proof. Anna owns the metric caveat; Jake and Priya own the product-truth lane.
checks.reason: The document states that 7-day activation is 19/27 and first live sync is 16/27, explains the three-account gap as real-source connections without a live sync in that window, defines activation as real source connection OR completed first live sync, and explicitly excludes sample imports, preview-only sessions, and invite-only activity.

input.body:
Archive note — for internal record. Captures the mechanism of the March 15, 2023 Scaffold production outage and the reasons its impact was uneven across tenants. Source: incident-response and retrospective memory; no customer-facing artifact.

Incident summary
- Date: Wednesday, March 15, 2023. Alert fired late afternoon Pacific time; the incident extended through the night and was fully recovered on March 16, 2023. End-to-end duration approximately 18 hours.
- Symptoms at the edge: spike in API 500 errors, many customer jobs simultaneously stuck in the queue. Staging was unaffected, so the failure was not reproducible pre-production.
- Response: Devon investigated traces and logs; Priya rolled traffic back from the edge feature flag. Rollback stopped new traffic from reaching the bad path, but already-queued work continued producing stragglers in the worker pool, which is why recovery was not instantaneous.

Root cause — what the change actually did
- A small diff of roughly ten lines was deployed behind a feature flag. The change introduced a new request path that was intended to bypass the old entitlement check.
- In production, requests on the new path missed the cache and fell through to the old entitlement check instead of taking the intended fast path.
- The old entitlement branch then retried the request against the worker pool. Each affected request expanded into approximately 6–8 internal calls, accumulating in the worker queue.
- Net effect: a small change in code produced a disproportionately large blast radius because the amplification (cache miss → entitlement retry → worker retry) happened inside the request-handling path, not at the edge.

Why the impact was uneven across tenants
- The faulty branch was not universally reachable. It was conditional on the new request path AND a cache miss AND the entitlement-check branch condition being met.
- Only the subset of tenants whose traffic hit that exact combination entered the amplification loop. Tenants on other paths, or with warm caches, were unaffected for the duration.
- This is the asymmetric blast radius: a path-conditional bug with multiplicative downstream retries, not a flat platform-wide failure.
- Dashboards appeared only partly degraded because aggregate metrics blended healthy and unhealthy tenant traffic. The partial degradation was visible longer than it should have been, which delayed the read that the edge was the place to act.

Why a ten-line change became an eighteen-hour incident
- The change shipped behind a flag without production-like replay, so the cache-miss + entitlement-branch combination had not been exercised against realistic traffic.
- The deploy landed late in the day, after most of the team had gone offline. Detection and response started from a thin on-call footprint.
- The rollback path was not immediately clear; once it was, edge-flag rollback cleared new traffic but the worker queue kept generating stragglers until it drained.

What changed after
- Standing rule: no branchy authentication or entitlement logic behind a feature flag unless it has been tested with production-like replay.
- Deploy discipline tightened; the late-Friday rule (no late-Friday production deploys unless the full team is on standby) was adopted later in direct response to this class of incident.
- A retrospective was held March 17, 2023 focused on merge timing, production access, and why the rollback path had been unclear.

Open gaps in the record
- The tenant set affected by the faulty branch is not named in available memory; if needed for a future customer conversation, that mapping would have to be reconstructed from queue and trace logs at the time.
- Staging did not reproduce the failure, which is itself the strongest argument for the production-like replay requirement that came out of the retrospective.

checks.observed:
Archive note — for internal record. Captures the mechanism of the March 15, 2023 Scaffold production outage and the reasons its impact was uneven across tenants. Source: incident-response and retrospective memory; no customer-facing artifact.

Incident summary
- Date: Wednesday, March 15, 2023. Alert fired late afternoon Pacific time; the incident extended through the night and was fully recovered on March 16, 2023. End-to-end duration approximately 18 hours.
- Symptoms at the edge: spike in API 500 errors, many customer jobs simultaneously stuck in the queue. Staging was unaffected, so the failure was not reproducible pre-production.
- Response: Devon investigated traces and logs; Priya rolled traffic back from the edge feature flag. Rollback stopped new traffic from reaching the bad path, but already-queued work continued producing stragglers in the worker pool, which is why recovery was not instantaneous.

Root cause — what the change actually did
- A small diff of roughly ten lines was deployed behind a feature flag. The change introduced a new request path that was intended to bypass the old entitlement check.
- In production, requests on the new path missed the cache and fell through to the old entitlement check instead of taking the intended fast path.
- The old entitlement branch then retried the request against the worker pool. Each affected request expanded into approximately 6–8 internal calls, accumulating in the worker queue.
- Net effect: a small change in code produced a disproportionately large blast radius because the amplification (cache miss → entitlement retry → worker retry) happened inside the request-handling path, not at the edge.

Why the impact was uneven across tenants
- The faulty branch was not universally reachable. It was conditional on the new request path AND a cache miss AND the entitlement-check branch condition being met.
- Only the subset of tenants whose traffic hit that exact combination entered the amplification loop. Tenants on other paths, or with warm caches, were unaffected for the duration.
- This is the asymmetric blast radius: a path-conditional bug with multiplicative downstream retries, not a flat platform-wide failure.
- Dashboards appeared only partly degraded because aggregate metrics blended healthy and unhealthy tenant traffic. The partial degradation was visible longer than it should have been, which delayed the read that the edge was the place to act.

Why a ten-line change became an eighteen-hour incident
- The change shipped behind a flag without production-like replay, so the cache-miss + entitlement-branch combination had not been exercised against realistic traffic.
- The deploy landed late in the day, after most of the team had gone offline. Detection and response started from a thin on-call footprint.
- The rollback path was not immediately clear; once it was, edge-flag rollback cleared new traffic but the worker queue kept generating stragglers until it drained.

What changed after
- Standing rule: no branchy authentication or entitlement logic behind a feature flag unless it has been tested with production-like replay.
- Deploy discipline tightened; the late-Friday rule (no late-Friday production deploys unless the full team is on standby) was adopted later in direct response to this class of incident.
- A retrospective was held March 17, 2023 focused on merge timing, production access, and why the rollback path had been unclear.

Open gaps in the record
- The tenant set affected by the faulty branch is not named in available memory; if needed for a future customer conversation, that mapping would have to be reconstructed from queue and trace logs at the time.
- Staging did not reproduce the failure, which is itself the strongest argument for the production-like replay requirement that came out of the retrospective.

Recapping what Acme could do at the May 21-22, 2025 checkpoint on the API v2 export timeout, before the later chunking/backoff patch and the August 2025 closeout.

- Two timeouts on Acme's long-range renewal-risk export on the cursor-paginated large-export path.

Happy to walk through the thread if useful.

Morgan
